newsitem.title: USA: Wisconsin Energy, Northern States merger on hold.
newsitem.headline: Wisconsin Energy, Northern States merger on hold.

text.p: A proposed merger between Wisconsin Energy Corp and Northern States Power Co is "on ice" until state regulators can meet with a Dane County Circuit Court judge on Thursday afternoon, Wisconsin Energy said on Tuesday.

"The merger is on ice," said Maripat Blankenheim, a spokeswoman for Wisconsin Energy. "As far as we're concerned, there will be no reassessment of our merger application. We'll just wait for a decision."
The utilities announced their merger proposal last May.
On Tuesday morning, Dane County Judge Richard Callaway issued a writ prohibiting regulators from deliberating on the $6.0 billion deal as originally planned.
Callaway's order followed reports last week in The Capital Times, a Madison, Wisconsin, newspaper, that Dane County District Attorney began a secret probe of the allegations.
Wisconsin Energy's Blankeneim said no one at the company has been contacted in the "John Doe" investigaiton.

The Wisconsin Public Service Commission is scheduled to meet on Thursday with Judge Mark Frankel. He is the original judge hearing lawsuits filed by two consumer advocate groups alleging improper contact between Wisconsin Energy and commission member Daniel Eastman.
A commission spokesman said Judge Callaway happened to be the judge on duty Tuesday.
"The question for Thursday," according to Douglas Fischer, an analyst at A.G. Edwards, "is whether the judge will lift the writ or let it remain in place."
"The commission could be in a position to approve the deal as early as Friday if he lifts the writ," Fischer said. "But we face some uncertainty if the writ stays in place."
Additionally, a statement released by the commission said "no factual allegations regarding 'ex parte' communications ... have ever been brought forward to this commission."
The outcome of Thursday's meeting is not only being scrutinized by officials of Milwaukee-based Wisconsin Energy and Northern States managers in Minneapolis.

"Utilities and the financial community are watching this very carefully," said Wisconsin Energy spokeswoman Blankenheim, "especially those who may want to sell energy once deregulation truly arrives."
